blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 3 - Fundamentals - Running tests from the CLI

By the end of this lesson you will have run a real spec from the command line, seen an
HTML report, and know the difference between `package.json` and `package-lock.json`.

> **Shell commands, not language syntax.** [Day 2](/learn/w1/d2/p2) got your environment
> ready. This is where you actually use it.

> **Partly here, partly in your own project.** The first cells run real terminal commands (like `runSpec` does under the
> hood); the rest is explore-mode as usual.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Goals** | `package.json` vs `package-lock.json`, and how to read a run's output |
| **Tools** | `npx playwright test` · `--headed` · `show-report` |
| **Environment** | here, though the first cells run real terminal commands |
| **Key takeaway** | Check the test count. This repo runs Chromium only, so the count is lower than a fresh scaffold's. |

## `package.json` vs `package-lock.json`

| File | What it holds | Do you edit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `package.json` | Your project's declared dependencies (version *ranges*), plus scripts like `npm test` | Yes — by hand, or via `npm install <pkg>` |
| `package-lock.json` | The *exact* resolved version of every dependency (and their dependencies), for a reproducible install | No — npm writes it; you just commit it |

`npm install` reads `package.json`, resolves versions, and writes/updates
`package-lock.json`. Committing the lock file is what guarantees your teammate — or CI —
installs the exact same versions you tested against.

## Running tests

```bash
npx playwright test                                    # run everything testMatch finds
npx playwright test week1/generated/day3-smoke.spec.ts  # run just this file
npx playwright test --headed                            # watch the browser while it runs
npx playwright show-report                               # open the last HTML report
```

`npx` runs the locally-installed `playwright` CLI (the one in `node_modules/.bin`) without
needing it installed globally.

## Example — run a real spec and read the output

There's no default example spec in this repo (a *fresh* `npm init playwright@latest` scaffold
ships one, but this shared repo doesn't keep one lying around) — so the cell below writes a
small, real smoke spec against the banking app, then runs it exactly the way `npx playwright
test` would from your terminal.

**Objective:** run a real spec via the CLI and read a real pass/fail report.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too**, exactly as you would on a real project:
> `npx playwright test week1/generated/day3-smoke.spec.ts`
> Try `--headed` once to watch it, then `npx playwright show-report` to open the HTML report.

**Expected result:** `2 passed`.

A note on the number: a *fresh* `npm init playwright@latest` scaffold runs every test against
**three** browser projects (chromium, firefox, webkit), so two tests there would report
`6 passed`. This repo's config runs **chromium only** by default (you saw the commented-out
`firefox`/`webkit` lines on [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2)) — so two tests here means `2 passed`, not 6. Same
mechanism, different project count. Week 3 Day 5 covers turning the other browsers back on.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same flow, a different check: write a spec that, after logging in, confirms the Payments tile is visible - not just that the login page loads.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Commit `package.json` **and** `package-lock.json` together, every time either changes.
- Prefer running one spec file while you're actively writing it (`npx playwright test
  path/to.spec.ts`); run the whole suite before you're done.
- `show-report` after any run that surprised you — the HTML report has the trace/screenshot
  a line of terminal output can't show.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Expecting "6 passed" like a fresh scaffold | Only chromium runs here — fewer results than you expected | Check `projects` in the config before assuming a browser count |
| Editing `package-lock.json` by hand | Installs drift, confusing "works on my machine" bugs | Never hand-edit it — let `npm install` write it |
| Forgetting `--headed` is a flag, not a default | Every run is headless and you can't see what's happening | Add `--headed` when you want to watch |
Two tests run here and report `2 passed`. The same two tests on a fresh `npm init playwright@latest` scaffold report `6 passed`. Why?

options: The scaffold retries each test twice by default
A fresh scaffold has three browser projects active, and every test runs once per project
The scaffold counts each `expect()` as a test
checkpoint.explanation: The `projects` array is the multiplier: chromium, firefox and webkit in a fresh scaffold, chromium alone here with the other two commented out. Same mechanism, different project count. Check `projects` before you trust a test count.

blocks.text: Which file do you never edit by hand, and why?

options: `package.json` — npm owns it, and hand edits are overwritten
`package-lock.json` — npm writes it, and hand edits make installs drift from what you tested
Both are generated and neither should be edited
checkpoint.explanation: `package.json` is yours: you declare dependencies and scripts in it. The lock file records the exact resolved version of everything underneath, which is what makes a teammate's install or a CI install match yours. You commit it; you do not write it.

blocks.text: A run behaved unexpectedly and the terminal output does not explain it. What does the lesson reach for?

options: `npx playwright show-report`, for the trace and screenshot the terminal cannot show
checkpoint.explanation: The HTML report carries the trace, screenshot and video that a line of terminal output cannot. `--headed` is for watching a run live, which is useful but different — and the report is already there after any run, with no re-run needed.

blocks.text:
- `npx` runs the locally installed CLI out of `node_modules/.bin`, so nothing needs installing globally.
- `package.json` is yours to edit; `package-lock.json` is npm's to write and yours to commit.
- Run one spec file while writing it; run the suite before you call it done.
- `--headed` to watch it happen, `show-report` to see what already happened.
- **The `projects` array multiplies your test count.** Check it before being surprised by a number.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3) takes a first, deliberately shallow look inside `playwright.config.ts`
itself.

# Week 1 - Day 3 - Implementation - A first look inside `playwright.config.ts`

By the end of this lesson you will recognize every top-level setting in this repo's real
config file and roughly what it does — not master any of them yet.

> **This is deliberately shallow, and that's flagged on purpose.** This slot usually shows
> the [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2) lesson's API wrapped in framework structure — but there's no framework yet, and this
> config file gets much deeper, dedicated treatment later: **week3/day1** covers timeouts in
> the config, and **week3/day5** covers `projects`/`workers`/`retries` properly, with
> measurements. Today is just: here's what's in the file, and roughly what each piece is for.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Scope** | Recognize every setting, without mastering any of them yet. Timeouts are covered in Week 3 - Day 1, and `projects`, `workers`, and `retries` in Week 3 - Day 5. |
| **Key takeaway** | `retain-on-failure` — keep the evidence only when something went wrong |

## The whole file, section by section

Open `playwright.config.ts` at the repo root. Here's what each top-level key is for:

| Setting | What you saw in this repo's file | Roughly means |
|---|---|---|
| `testDir` / `testMatch` | `"./"` and `["week*/**/*.spec.ts", ...]` | Where to look for spec files (you read this on [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2)) |
| `fullyParallel` | `true` | Run tests in the same file in parallel, not just across files |
| `forbidOnly` | `!!process.env.CI` | In CI, refuse to run if anyone left a `.only` in a spec |
| `retries` | `process.env.CI ? 2 : 0` | Re-run a failed test this many times before calling it failed — locally: never |
| `reporter` | `[["html", ...], ["list"]]` | Two reporters at once: an HTML report file, and live output in the terminal |
| `use` | see below | Shared settings every test gets, unless overridden |
| `projects` | one entry per browser | Which browser(s) each test runs against |

## The `use` block

| Setting | Value here | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `baseURL` | the banking app's URL | Lets a test write `page.goto("/")` instead of the full URL |
| `trace` | `"retain-on-failure"` | Records a full trace (DOM snapshots, network, console) — but only keeps it if the test fails |
| `screenshot` | `"only-on-failure"` | Same idea, for a screenshot |
| `video` | `"retain-on-failure"` | Same idea, for a video recording |

`retain-on-failure` is the setting worth remembering as "the recommended default" — recording
everything, always, is expensive; recording nothing means a CI failure you can't diagnose.
Keeping evidence **only when something went wrong** is the sweet spot.

**Expected result:** the object printed with four keys. Notice all three artifact settings
(`trace`/`screenshot`/`video`) use the same "only keep it on failure" shape — that's a
pattern, not three separate decisions.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same idea, a different field: as plain data, write what the `use` block would look like with `headless: false` added to it.

blocks.text:
## `projects`

```ts
projects: [
  { name: "chromium", use: { ...devices["Desktop Chrome"] } },
  // { name: "firefox", use: { ...devices["Desktop Firefox"] } },
  // { name: "webkit", use: { ...devices["Desktop Safari"] } },
],
```

One entry per browser you want to test against. Each test in your suite runs once per
active project — which is exactly why the [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2) lesson's two tests only ran twice: one project
(chromium) is active, the other two are commented out.

**We'll go much deeper on `projects` — plus `workers` and `retries` — in week3/day5**, with
measured test counts and real cross-browser runs. For today, just recognize that the array's
*length* is what multiplies your test count.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same idea, a different field again: this time add a `retries` value alongside the existing options, as plain data.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Read `projects` before you're surprised by a test count — it's the single biggest
  multiplier in any report.
- Leave `retries` at 0 locally; let CI (`process.env.CI`) be the only place it turns on.
- Don't touch `trace`/`screenshot`/`video` settings without a reason — `retain-on-failure` is
  the default worth keeping.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Assumed all 3 browsers run | Confused by a lower test count than expected | Check which `projects` entries are actually uncommented |
| Thought `trace: "retain-on-failure"` records every run | Missing traces on a passing test you wanted to inspect | It's by design — force one with `--trace on` for a single run if you need it |
| Looked for `workers` and didn't find it here | Assumed it wasn't configurable | It's a real setting, just not set in this file — Playwright picks a sensible default. week3/day5 covers it. |
`trace`, `screenshot` and `video` are all set to keep artifacts only on failure. Why not simply record everything?

options: Recording every run is expensive, and recording nothing leaves a CI failure you cannot diagnose. Keeping the evidence only on failure balances the two
Playwright cannot record a trace for a passing test
Because artifacts from passing tests would be committed to git
checkpoint.explanation: All three settings share one shape, which makes it a single decision rather than three. The cost is real on a big suite, and the evidence is only ever wanted for the runs that went wrong. `--trace on` forces a recording for one run when you do want it.

blocks.text: `retries` is set to `process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`. What does that mean when you run locally?

options: Two retries, the same as CI
No retries at all — a failure is reported the first time it happens
Retries are disabled everywhere; the expression is a placeholder
checkpoint.explanation: Locally you want a failure to show itself immediately rather than being hidden by a re-run. CI is the place to absorb an infrastructure problem. Retries hiding a real flake on your own machine is exactly what this avoids.

blocks.text:
- `testDir`/`testMatch` find the specs; `projects` decides which browsers, and multiplies the count.
- `use` holds what every test gets by default — `baseURL` is why `page.goto("/")` works.
- `retain-on-failure` for trace, screenshot and video: one decision, three settings.
- `retries` on in CI, off locally. `forbidOnly` stops a stray `.only` passing CI on one test.
- Today is recognition, not mastery. Week 3 takes the same file apart with measurements.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w1/d3/p4) — practice reading this config for real.
[Day 4](/learn/w1/d4/p2) — Codegen and finding locators the right way.

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 3 - Practice - Running tests & the config file

Three problems, using the real CLI and the real config — nothing invented.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | the real CLI and the real config, nothing invented |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2) for the commands · [Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3) for the settings |
| **Environment** | Run Problem 1 yourself with `--headed`, in your own project rather than the studio's test runner. |

## When you're done

You can now run a suite, read its report, and recognize every top-level setting in the
config. [Day 4](/learn/w1/d4/p2) is where you learn to *find* the locators that go inside a
test, using Codegen.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Run `week1/generated/day3-smoke.spec.ts` yourself from a real terminal
(not through `runSpec`) with `--headed`, and watch the browser open. Then run
`npx playwright show-report` and find the two test results in the HTML report.

**Where.** Your terminal (VS Code's integrated terminal is fine).

**How you'll know it worked.** You saw a real Chromium window open and close, and the HTML
report opened in your browser showing 2 passed tests.
problems.stub: // Problem 1 — no code needed here; do this in your terminal, then note what you saw.
problems.solution:
**This one is done in your own terminal** — the studio's Run button drives the Playwright *library*, not the test runner, so there is no headed window to watch here.

```bash
npx playwright test week1/generated/day3-smoke.spec.ts --headed
```
```bash
npx playwright show-report
```

**What you should have seen**

- A real Chromium window opening, driving the app at visible speed, and closing again. `--headed` is the flag; without it the same run happens invisibly.
- `npx playwright show-report` opening `playwright-report/index.html` in your browser, with both test results listed, each expandable to its step-by-step log.

**Why the lesson asks.** Two things become concrete the first time you watch it: the browser really is being driven rather than simulated, and the HTML report is generated on *every* run, not only on failure. From here on, "what actually happened" is a report you open, not a guess.

> If the window flashed past too quickly, add `--slow-mo=500` — but reach for the trace, not slow-mo, once you are debugging a real failure.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Open this repo's real `playwright.config.ts` and answer, from what's
actually in the file:

1. What does `retries` evaluate to when you run locally (not in CI)?
2. Name the three `use` settings that are all set to `"retain-on-failure"` or
   `"only-on-failure"`.
3. How many `projects` entries are active (uncommented) right now?

**Where.** A cell in this lesson, as comments.

**How you'll know it worked.** All three answers match the actual file, not the [Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3) lesson's summary
of it.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Read them out of the file rather than from memory.

> 1. **`retries`** — the generated config reads `retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`, so locally it evaluates to **0**. A failure on your machine is a failure, immediately; only CI gets a second and third attempt. That asymmetry is deliberate — retries hide flakiness, and you want it visible while you are writing.
> 2. **The three evidence settings in `use`** — `trace`, `screenshot` and `video`. In the course repo they are set to retain or capture only on failure, so a green run leaves nothing behind and a red one leaves everything you need.
> 3. **Active `projects`** — **one**: `chromium`. Firefox and WebKit are in the file but commented out.

**What makes an answer good** is that each came from a line you can point at. The `retries` one especially: plenty of people assume retries are on everywhere and are then surprised that CI is greener than their laptop.

> Needs the training repo on your own machine.

problems.statement:
There's no framework-shaped code yet for a true advanced problem, so instead: imagine you're
handed a **brand-new, empty project** tomorrow. Using what you now know about `projects`,
`retries`, and the `use` block, write down the config choices you'd start with and why —
would you turn on all three browsers immediately, or start with one? Would you leave
`retries: 0` locally? What would you set `trace`/`screenshot`/`video` to?

**Where.** A cell in this lesson, as comments — no code to run.

**How you'll know it worked.** Every choice has a one-line reason attached, not just a
preference.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** A defensible starting config for a brand-new suite, with the reasoning attached:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'https://staging.example.com',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
  projects: [{ name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } }],
});
```

> **One browser to begin with.** Chromium only. Cross-browser coverage matters, but on a suite that is two weeks old nearly every failure is your own bug, and three browsers means triaging each one three times.
>
> **`retries: 0` locally, 2 in CI.** Keep flakiness in your face while you are writing; absorb genuine infrastructure blips on the shared runner. A test that only passes on the second attempt is information, and CI records that.
>
> **Evidence on failure only.** Traces and videos on every green run are gigabytes of artefacts nobody opens.
>
> **`baseURL` from the environment.** The one setting guaranteed to differ between your machine, staging and CI. Hard-coding it is the first thing you will regret.

**The shape of a good answer** is that every line has a reason. You revisit all of this properly in Week 3 — timeouts on Day 1, projects and workers on Day 5.
